Daktronics, Inc. is an American manufacturer of electronic scoreboards, LED video
displays, and related timing, scoring, and messaging systems, based in Brookings,
South Dakota. Founded in 1968 by two South Dakota State University engineering
professors, it is a publicly traded company (NASDAQ: DAKT) and one of the principal
suppliers of large electronic displays worldwide. Within aquatics it long supplied
swim-timing consoles, touchpads, and start systems built around its OmniSport
consoles, but it has since wound that line down; its current aquatic offering is
mainly scoreboards and video displays.[^wiki][^about][^swimsw]

Part of the Daktronics hardware documented in the
[equipment reference](../equipment/index.md) is
aquatic timing gear built around the company's OmniSport timing consoles.

## History

Daktronics was founded in 1968 by Aelred J. Kurtenbach and Duane Sander, both
electrical-engineering professors at South Dakota State University; the name is a
contraction of "Dakota" and "electronics." An early aim was to keep engineering
graduates employed in South Dakota.[^wiki][^fund] The company raised its first capital
through a local stock offering in 1969, and in 1970 delivered its first product, an
electronic voting-display system for the Utah state legislature.[^fund]

Its move into sports came after South Dakota State University's wrestling coach asked
for a better scoreboard; that wrestling scoreboard led to a broader line of
programmable displays. A Daktronics scoreboard was used at wrestling during the 1976
Summer Olympics, and the company supplied displays for the 1980 Winter Olympics at
Lake Placid, by which point annual sales had passed one million dollars.[^wiki][^fund]

Daktronics listed on the NASDAQ market under the ticker DAKT in 1994 and expanded into
video displays, digital billboards, dynamic message signs, and sound systems, with
manufacturing in Brookings and additional facilities in Sioux Falls, Redwood Falls
(Minnesota), and overseas.[^wiki][^about] The company describes itself as employing more
than 2,500 people with displays in over 120 countries; its fiscal-year 2024 reporting
listed 2,422 employees and revenue of about 756 million dollars, so the marketing
"2,500+" figure is somewhat higher than the reported headcount.[^about][^wiki]

## Products

Daktronics designs, manufactures, sells, and services electronic display, timing, and
scoring equipment across many sports, with a dedicated aquatics line.[^about][^aquatics]

- Scoreboards & video displays, fixed-digit scoreboards in multisport, swimming,
  water-polo, and auxiliary configurations, and full-color LED video boards. Aquatic
  models use a silicone coating to protect the LEDs from pool moisture.[^aquatics]
- Aquatic timing & scoring, the OmniSport timing-console line and its touchpads,
  start systems, and relay platforms for swimming, diving, water polo, and
  synchronized (artistic) swimming, interfacing to meet-management software such as
  Hy-Tek Meet Manager. Daktronics has since discontinued this swim-timing line (see
  [In swim timing](#in-swim-timing)).[^aquatics][^omni][^swimsw]
- Other sports, beyond aquatics Daktronics supplies scoreboards, timing, and video
  displays for sports including football, basketball, baseball, hockey, and
  track.[^about]

Individual Daktronics aquatic products are catalogued in the
[equipment reference](../equipment/index.md): the
[OmniSport 2000](../equipment/swimming/timers/omnisport-2000.md) timing console,
the head end of a Daktronics swim-timing system, and the earlier
[OmniSport 1000](../equipment/swimming/timers/omnisport-1000.md) and
[OmniSport 6000](../equipment/swimming/timers/omnisport-6000.md) consoles it
succeeded, together with the
[T-7000 series touchpads](../equipment/swimming/touchpad/t-7000.md) that sense each
lane's finish, the
[backup pushbutton](../equipment/swimming/semi-automatic/pushbutton/daktronics.md) that backs it up,
the [RTOP relay take-off platforms](../equipment/swimming/relay-judging/daktronics.md)
that judge relay exchanges from the blocks, the
[HS-200 Horn Start](../equipment/swimming/starter/hs-200.md) that starts the race,
and the [lane speakers](../equipment/swimming/external-speaker/daktronics.md) mounted
under each block. Scoreboard models are added as those pages are written.

## In swim timing

Daktronics is one of a small number of major aquatic-timing and scoring
manufacturers, alongside [Colorado Time Systems](colorado-time-systems.md),
[Swiss Timing](swiss-timing.md) (Omega), and [Seiko](seiko.md).[^wiki-timing] Its aquatics offering centers on the OmniSport 2000 console, which
collects finish signals from in-lane touchpads and backup buttons, receives the start
pulse, runs the race clock, drives the scoreboard, and prints results, and which also
scores judged diving and water polo through wired and wireless judge
consoles.[^omni][^aquatics]

Daktronics has largely withdrawn from swim timing. Its two earlier consoles, the
[OmniSport 1000](../equipment/swimming/timers/omnisport-1000.md) and
[OmniSport 6000](../equipment/swimming/timers/omnisport-6000.md), are discontinued
and no longer documented by the company. The OmniSport 2000 is still listed on an
active support page, but its ProSwimming, ProDiving, and ProSyncro software interfaces
are discontinued and no longer available for purchase, with Daktronics directing
customers to its professional services rather than selling new swim-timing software;
the aquatic touchpads, relay take-off platforms, and start systems likewise appear
among the company's discontinued-product resources.[^swimsw][^omni] Installed OmniSport
2000 consoles are still supported, and Daktronics continues to make aquatic scoreboards
and video displays, but it no longer markets a current swim-timing system.[^omni][^aquatics]

## In competition

Daktronics scoreboards and video displays have been used at multiple Olympic Games,
including the 1976 Summer Olympics, the 1980 Winter Olympics at Lake Placid, and later
Summer Games, and are widely installed in collegiate, professional, and municipal
venues.[^wiki][^fund] The company says it has manufactured tens of thousands of video
displays for customers in more than 120 countries.[^about]
